candidates.explanation: The refresh token is signed with expiresIn read from 'auth.expires' (the short access-token lifetime) instead of 'auth.refreshExpires' (AUTH_REFRESH_TOKEN_EXPIRES_IN). So the refresh token expires minutes after issue and /auth/refresh returns 401 once that time passes.

fix.description: Use the refresh expiry config key when signing the refresh token.

candidates.explanation: updateByHash ignores conditions.hash. It updates the session by id only, so any refresh token for that session passes the check, even one carrying a stale hash. The hash is rotated on each refresh, but the old token's hash is never compared with the stored one, so the old refresh token can be replayed. The document (Mongo) repository does match on hash and is correct.

fix.description: Include the hash in the update's where clause so the update only affects the row when the presented hash matches the stored one. Then `affected` is 0 for a stale token and the service throws Unauthorized. Because the check and the update are one statement, concurrent replays also can't both succeed.

candidates.explanation: The duplicate-email check uses `userByEmail.id === currentUser.id`. This is the wrong comparison. The email is already known to differ from the current user's email, so a match on the current user's id is practically impossible. An email that belongs to another account has a different id, so the check is false and no 422 `emailExists` is thrown. The code goes on to sign the confirmation hash and send the confirmation mail, and the request returns 200. The condition should be `userByEmail.id !== currentUser.id`, or simply `userByEmail`.

fix.description: Change the condition on line 483 to `if (userByEmail && userByEmail.id !== currentUser.id)` so that an email owned by a different user throws the 422 emailExists error.

candidates.explanation: When no user matches the social id but a user with the same email exists, the code links the social login to that account only if it is not inactive. The condition is inverted. For an active password account it overwrites provider with 'google' and sets socialId. After that, the email login at line 51 rejects the user with needLoginViaProvider:google. Social sign-in should not take over an active email account. The code should leave an existing email-provider account's provider and socialId unchanged, or reject the login with a conflict error.

fix.description: In the userByEmail branch, do not overwrite provider and socialId on an existing account. If the existing account's provider is email and it is active, throw an UnprocessableEntityException (for example email: 'emailAlreadyExistsWithEmailProvider'). Otherwise keep the existing behaviour for accounts that are not password accounts.

candidates.explanation: The duplicate-email check is inverted. It throws emailExists only when the user found by the new email is the current user (`===`). That can't normally happen, because this block only runs when the email differs from the current one. When the email belongs to a different account, the check is skipped. The code then signs a confirm-email hash and sends the mail, and the endpoint returns 200.

fix.description: Change the condition to `if (userByEmail && userByEmail.id !== currentUser.id)`. Alternatively, throw whenever `userByEmail` exists, since the email is already known to differ from the current one.

candidates.explanation: updateByHash ignores conditions.hash. The UPDATE only filters on { id }, so any refresh token for the session (including an already-rotated one with a stale hash) still matches, overwrites the hash and returns the session. Replaying the old refresh token therefore yields a new token pair. The hash comparison that should invalidate rotated tokens is never done.

fix.description: Include the hash in the update's where clause so that only the current hash matches, e.g. update({ id: Number(conditions.id), hash: conditions.hash }, { hash: payload.hash }). A stale token then affects 0 rows and returns null, which makes refreshToken throw UnauthorizedException.

candidates.explanation: The refresh token is signed with expiresIn from 'auth.expires' (the short access-token lifetime) instead of 'auth.refreshExpires' (AUTH_REFRESH_TOKEN_EXPIRES_IN). So the refresh token's exp is only minutes after iat, and /auth/refresh returns 401 once that lifetime passes, regardless of the 30d setting.

fix.description: Use the refresh expiry config when signing the refresh token: replace getOrThrow('auth.expires') at line 632 with getOrThrow('auth.refreshExpires', { infer: true }).

candidates.explanation: The spread order is reversed: `{ ...payload, ...UserMapper.toDomain(entity) }`. The existing entity values are spread last and overwrite the incoming payload (firstName, lastName, role, etc.). The save call therefore writes the old values back. The request returns 200 with the unchanged user and the database doesn't change. The document repository does it correctly, with the payload spread last.

fix.description: Spread the existing entity first and the payload last, so the payload overrides the stored values: UserMapper.toPersistence({ ...UserMapper.toDomain(entity), ...payload })

candidates.explanation: The comment says the secret embeds the current password hash, so a reset link stops verifying once the password changes. The code instead appends user.email, which does not change when the password is reset. The JWT therefore still verifies after use and stays valid until it expires, so the same link can set a password repeatedly.

Nothing invalidates the token after a successful reset. Verification uses only the email-based secret, and the code stores no used-token marker. The user's password is overwritten and sessions are deleted, but the reset JWT stays valid.

fix.description: Make getForgotSecret derive the secret from the user's current password hash, for example `${forgotSecret}${user.password ?? ''}`. Use it in both signing and verification, as the code already does. The stored hash changes on reset, so old links fail verification. Make sure resetPassword loads the user with the password hash populated. If the user entity's password column is not selected or is excluded, load it explicitly.

candidates.explanation: The duplicate-email check uses `userByEmail.id === currentUser.id`. That is true only when the email belongs to the current user, which can't happen inside the `email !== currentUser.email` branch. When the email belongs to a different account, the ids differ, so the check is false. No 422 `emailExists` is thrown, and the code goes on to sign the confirmation hash and send the mail, so the request returns 200. The comparison should be `!==`.

fix.description: Change the condition to `if (userByEmail && userByEmail.id !== currentUser.id)`, so the 422 emailExists is thrown when the email belongs to another user.

So the refresh JWT's exp is only minutes after iat, and /auth/refresh rejects it with 401 once the access-token lifetime has passed.

fix.description: Use the refresh expiry config key when signing the refresh token: replace getOrThrow('auth.expires') with getOrThrow('auth.refreshExpires', { infer: true }) in the refresh token signAsync options.

candidates.explanation: The merge order is wrong. `{...payload, ...UserMapper.toDomain(entity)}` spreads the existing entity after the payload, so the stored firstName, lastName and role overwrite the incoming changes. The save then writes the unchanged values. The request still returns 200 with the old data, and the database does not change. The document repository spreads the existing user first and the payload second, which is the correct order.

fix.description: Spread the existing entity first and the payload second, so that the payload overrides the stored values: `{...UserMapper.toDomain(entity), ...clonedPayload}`. Remove `id` from the payload first, as the document repository does.

candidates.explanation: When a social login has no matching social id but the email matches an existing user, the code overwrites that user's provider and socialId with the social ones if the user is not inactive. An active, confirmed email/password account therefore gets provider=google. The email login check at line 51 (user.provider !== email) then returns needLoginViaProvider:google. The social sign-in takes over the active password account instead of being rejected or leaving the account untouched.

fix.description: In the `else if (userByEmail)` branch, do not mutate provider/socialId of an existing account registered with a different provider (especially an active email/password one). Throw a 422 (e.g. errors: { email: 'emailAlreadyExists' } or 'needLoginViaProvider:email'), or sign in without persisting a provider change. Account linking should be an explicit authenticated action.

candidates.explanation: The merged object is `{...payload, ...UserMapper.toDomain(entity)}`. The existing DB entity is spread last, so its old values override every field in the update payload (firstName, lastName, role, etc.). The save call then writes the unchanged values and returns them. The request gets 200 OK, but nothing changes in the database.

fix.description: Spread the existing domain user first and the payload last, so the payload overrides the old values: `{...UserMapper.toDomain(entity), ...payload}`.

candidates.explanation: The comment says the reset-JWT secret embeds the current password hash, which would invalidate links once the password changes. The code instead returns forgotSecret + user.email, and the email never changes on a reset. The old token therefore still verifies after a successful reset, so the same link can be used repeatedly until it expires.

After verifying the hash, the method sets the new password but does nothing to invalidate the token, such as a stored nonce or a secret tied to the password hash. Because the verification secret doesn't change, the link stays valid.

fix.description: Make the secret depend on the user's current password hash, as the comment intends: return `${forgotSecret}${user.password ?? ''}`. The findById result must include the password hash. Alternatively, store a one-time token or nonce and clear it after the reset.

The hash is never compared with the stored value, so replaying the old refresh token succeeds and issues a new token pair. The document (Mongo) repository does filter on hash, which confirms the relational version is wrong.

The comment says it embeds the current password hash, so a link would stop verifying once the password changes. The email never changes when the password is reset, so the JWT still verifies after use and stays valid until it expires. The same link can then set another password.

fix.description: Include the user's current password hash in the secret, for example `${forgotSecret}${user.password ?? ''}`. Make sure findById returns the password field. Alternatively, store and invalidate a one-time token nonce when the password is reset.

fix.description: Include the user's current password hash in the signing secret, for example `${forgotSecret}${user.password ?? ''}`. Once the password changes, old reset tokens fail verification. Optionally also include the email.

candidates.explanation: updateByHash takes a conditions object with both id and hash, but the relational implementation filters only on `{ id: Number(conditions.id) }`. It ignores `conditions.hash`. After a refresh the session hash changes, but a replayed old refresh token (carrying the old hash) still matches the session by id. The update succeeds and a new token pair is issued. The document (Mongo) implementation correctly filters on both `_id` and `hash`.

Rotation relies entirely on updateByHash returning null when the presented hash doesn't match the current session hash. Because the repository ignores the hash, this check never rejects a stale refresh token.

fix.description: Include the hash in the update's where clause so that a stale hash affects no rows and updateByHash returns null: `update({ id: Number(conditions.id), hash: conditions.hash }, { hash: payload.hash })`.

candidates.explanation: When no user matches the social id and a user exists with the same email, the code overwrites user.provider and user.socialId whenever the user is not inactive. An active, confirmed email/password account therefore gets linked and converted to the social provider (provider becomes 'google'). validateLogin then rejects email login because user.provider !== 'email'. The condition only excludes inactive users, which is inverted or insufficient. It should not modify an existing active account of a different provider.

fix.description: In the `else if (userByEmail)` branch, do not overwrite provider or socialId on an existing active account. Either reject the social login with an error such as emailAlreadyExists, or sign the user in without changing provider and socialId. Only touch accounts that are not already active, for example inactive accounts that were never confirmed, and do so deliberately. Do not call update on an active email account.

candidates.explanation: The duplicate-email check is inverted. It throws emailExists only when the user found by the new email is the current user (`userByEmail.id === currentUser.id`). That can't happen here, because the new email differs from the current one. When the email belongs to a different account, the check passes. The code then signs a confirmation hash and sends the mail, and the request returns 200 instead of 422.

fix.description: Change the condition to `userByEmail && userByEmail.id !== currentUser.id`, or simply `if (userByEmail)`, so that an email owned by another account triggers the 422 emailExists error.

candidates.explanation: When no user matches the social id but one matches the email, the code overwrites that user's provider and socialId with the social ones. The guard `status !== inactive` is inverted. It applies the takeover to active, confirmed password accounts, so the provider becomes 'google'. The email login at auth.service.ts line 51 then rejects the account with needLoginViaProvider:google. The takeover should not happen for active email accounts. At most, an unconfirmed (inactive) account might be adopted.

fix.description: In the `else if (userByEmail)` branch, do not change provider or socialId on an existing active account. Either reject the login with an error such as `emailAlreadyRegistered` or `needLoginViaProvider:email`, or just log the user in without changing provider and socialId. Only treat the account as adoptable if it is inactive (unconfirmed), and ideally don't even do that.

candidates.explanation: When no user matches the social id and provider but one matches the verified email (`userByEmail`), the code overwrites `provider` and `socialId` on that existing account. It does this unless the account is inactive, and the status check is backwards. An active, confirmed email/password account therefore gets `provider='google'` and the Google `socialId`. The email login path then rejects it with 'needLoginViaProvider google'. Social sign-in should not take over an active password account. Nothing in this branch checks whether the account already has a different provider such as 'email'.

fix.description: In the `else if (userByEmail)` branch, stop mutating `provider` and `socialId` on an existing account that has a different provider. For a password account (`userByEmail.provider === 'email'`), either reject the login with a conflict error such as `emailAlreadyExists` or `needLoginViaProvider`, or sign in without changing the provider. Do not overwrite the provider on active password accounts. Only adopt or link accounts that have no usable credentials.

candidates.explanation: updateByHash is supposed to rotate the session hash only if the supplied hash matches the stored one. The relational implementation ignores conditions.hash: it updates WHERE id = conditions.id only. A replayed old refresh token (stale hash) therefore still matches the session, and the hash is overwritten again. The result is that a fresh token pair is issued every time. The document (Mongo) implementation correctly filters on both _id and hash.

fix.description: Include the hash in the update's where clause so a stale hash affects 0 rows and returns null. refreshToken then throws UnauthorizedException.

candidates.explanation: The merge order is reversed: `{ ...payload, ...UserMapper.toDomain(entity) }`. The existing DB entity is spread last, so its values override every field in the payload (firstName, lastName, role, and so on). The save then writes the old values back, and the endpoint returns 200 with the unchanged user. The document repository does this correctly, with the existing user first and the payload second.

fix.description: Spread the existing entity first and the payload last, so the payload overrides the stored values: `UserMapper.toPersistence({ ...UserMapper.toDomain(entity), ...payload })`. UsersService.update passes undefined for fields that were not supplied, and those would overwrite existing values. To avoid that, strip undefined keys from the payload before merging.

candidates.explanation: The comment says the per-user JWT secret embeds the current password hash so reset links stop verifying once the password changes. The code actually returns `forgotSecret + user.email`. Changing the password doesn't change the secret, so a used reset token still verifies until it expires. The same link can then be used to set another password.

After verification, the token is not invalidated in any way. There is no stored single-use marker and nothing else ties the token to the password state. So it relies entirely on getForgotSecret changing after the password update, and that doesn't happen.

fix.description: Include the user's current password hash in the signing secret, e.g. `return `${forgotSecret}${user.password ?? ''}`;`. This requires that usersService.findById returns the password field. Use the same value in forgotPassword and resetPassword. Once the password changes, old tokens fail verification.
